Appendix Table S2. Documentation completeness by caller scenario

Documentation completeness differed by arm in the same direction as the exploratory outcome. Because the derived availability outcome is read off the appointment date, a call recorded less completely is scored as less available regardless of what the practice said. Differential documentation and differential availability cannot be separated in these data.

Table S2. Documentation completeness by caller scenario.
Scenario Calls placed No call date Reached staff No appointment date
Straight couple 77 6 (7.8%) 39 11 (28.2%)
Lesbian couple 83 19 (22.9%) 37 23 (62.2%)
Single mother 74 12 (16.2%) 32 17 (53.1%)

Appendix Table S4. STROBE checklist for cross-sectional studies

Table S4. Completed STROBE checklist.
Item Section Recommendation Study response
1a Title and abstract Indicate the design in the title or abstract Title and abstract identify this as a national secret-shopper (audit) study.
1b Title and abstract Balanced summary of what was done and found Structured abstract reports the service menu as primary and states that the access comparison was uninformative.
2 Introduction Scientific background and rationale RRM service scope determines which patients can be served; national data were previously absent.
3 Introduction State specific objectives and any prespecified hypotheses Primary: define the service menu. Secondary and exploratory: access by caller scenario. No power analysis was prespecified in the protocol; achieved precision is reported instead.
4 Methods Present key elements of study design early Cross-sectional audit; each practice eligible for one call per scenario.
5 Methods Setting, locations, and relevant dates United States, 2025-2026; RRM practices compiled from professional directories.
6 Methods Eligibility criteria and selection National roster of RRM practices; call dispositions mapped to standard access-audit exclusion codes.
7 Methods Define all outcomes, exposures, predictors, confounders Primary outcome: reported service menu. Secondary: appointment availability inferred from call documentation, strict and broad definitions. Reached and offer-eligible are distinct denominators.
8 Methods Sources of data and measurement Trained callers using standardized scripts; responses entered in REDCap (pid 39546).
9 Methods Describe any efforts to address potential sources of bias Within-practice matched design for the secondary outcome; caller-overlap analysis reports which contrasts can be separated from caller effects; duplicate practice-scenario cells handled by a prespecified rule with first-vs-last sensitivity.
10 Methods Explain how the study size was arrived at No a priori sample-size calculation was performed. The achievable sample was the national roster of RRM practices. Minimum detectable effects are reported for every paired contrast.
11 Methods Explain how quantitative variables were handled Proportions with 95% Wilson or Clopper-Pearson intervals; wait time in business days, log-transformed and reported as geometric mean ratios.
12 Methods Statistical methods, subgroups, missing data, sensitivity Exact McNemar for matched contrasts; mixed-effects logistic regression with practice random intercept; two-part hurdle model for wait; Mantel-Haenszel stratification where caller overlap permits. Missingness by arm reported in Appendix Table S2.
13 Results Report numbers at each stage 234 calls placed, 108 reached a live office, 98 completed the service interview; Figures 2 and 3.
14 Results Characteristics of study participants Practice-level characteristics and per-scenario cascade in Table 1 and Figure 3.
15 Results Report numbers of outcome events or summary measures Service prevalences in Figure 1 and Appendix Table S3.
16 Results Give unadjusted and, if applicable, adjusted estimates with precision All estimates reported with 95% confidence intervals. P-values are not reported for the exploratory access contrasts, with the reason stated in the text.
17 Results Report other analyses done Strict vs broad availability, first-vs-last duplicate-call sensitivity, caller-stratified Mantel-Haenszel estimate.
18 Discussion Summarise key results with reference to objectives Primary finding is the structural absence of donor-gamete and ART services.
19 Discussion Discuss limitations, including bias and imprecision Derived availability outcome; caller-scenario confounding with no within-caller information for two of three contrasts; documentation completeness differing by arm; low reachability; single call per scenario.
20 Discussion Cautious overall interpretation The service finding is stated as structural; the access comparison is stated as uninformative rather than null.
21 Discussion Generalisability Findings describe the reachable subset of RRM practices nationally.
22 Other Give the source of funding No external funding; COMIRB 25-2596.

Appendix Table S5. Duplicate practice-scenario calls and their adjudication

The protocol specifies one call per practice per scenario. Eight cells contained two. Where a contact attempt (voicemail, wrong number, abandoned or over-long hold) preceded a completed call, the completed call determined the cell. Where two protocol-valid completed calls existed, the cell was treated as a protocol deviation and excluded from the primary paired analysis rather than resolved by preferring the earlier or later call. Practice identifiers are redacted.

Appendix Table S6. Restriction checkbox, why it is excluded

The instrument’s three “restrictions to the individuals you would provide care to” checkboxes are excluded from every analysis. The codebook defines a ticked box as a restriction applying to that group, with no field note or branching logic, but the recorded responses follow two incompatible conventions keyed to the person completing the form. One caller ticked all three boxes on most of her entries, which under the codebook definition would mean those practices serve no one. Every other caller ticked only the box matching the scenario they called as, which echoes the assignment rather than describing the practice. Because the convention belongs to the caller rather than the response, and a quarter of calls record no caller, no recoding rule can separate them.
